Trying to Conceive

Pregnancy after POI: own eggs, donor treatment and choices

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A diagnosis of premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) can change plans for a family without making every route to parenthood impossible. Some people retain intermittent ovarian activity; others consider previously stored eggs or embryos, donor treatment or another path. A useful consultation explains what is medically possible, what remains uncertain and what fits your wishes, without pressure to choose donation or keep trying indefinitely.

First, clarify what the diagnosis means

POI means loss of ovarian activity before age 40, usually with irregular or absent periods and abnormal hormone results. It is different from simply having a low ovarian-reserve result, and from an ovulation disorder such as PCOS/PMOS. Ask what established your diagnosis, what causes have been considered and whether genetic counselling would help.

Assessment considers your history, symptoms, pregnancy possibility and medicines. AMH alone cannot diagnose POI or predict a personal pregnancy chance. Hormonal medicines can affect bleeding and test results, so arrange a testing plan rather than stopping them yourself. You can request fertility advice as soon as POI is suspected or confirmed; there is no need to wait through ordinary trying-to-conceive intervals.

Can pregnancy still happen with my own eggs?

In non-surgical POI, ovarian activity and occasional ovulation can occur. Natural pregnancy is substantially less likely, but not always impossible. Removal of both ovaries is different: new eggs cannot be released from ovaries that are no longer present. A return of bleeding does not establish reliable ovulation or mean POI has been cured.

No intervention has reliably been shown to restore ovarian activity and natural conception rates in POI. Hormone replacement is not proof of fertility recovery. A specialist can discuss whether any monitored attempt using remaining own eggs is reasonable, including cancellation and a very low chance of success. A historical 5–10% figure cannot predict your outcome, and optimism is not a treatment requirement.

Previously frozen eggs or embryos may offer an option

If your own eggs or embryos were stored before ovarian damage, they may still be usable after POI. Stored eggs must survive warming, be fertilised and develop into suitable embryos; stored embryos also need to survive warming and continue developing. Age when eggs were collected, the number and quality stored, sperm factors and the laboratory all influence the outlook. Storage never guarantees a birth.

After cancer treatment, coordinate decisions with oncology and fertility specialists, including when pregnancy or treatment is appropriate and whether carrying a pregnancy is safe. Some people with residual function can discuss preservation after treatment, but it is not available to everyone with established POI. Previously stored ovarian tissue requires separate specialist assessment, including the risk of returning cancer cells; it is not an ordinary substitute for frozen eggs.

How treatment with donor eggs works

Donor eggs can be fertilised in the laboratory with a partner’s or donor’s sperm, followed by transfer of a suitable embryo to the uterus. A recipient generally does not need her own ovaries to produce eggs for this route, but needs an individual plan for the uterine lining, hormone support and follow-up. Fresh and frozen donor eggs involve different scheduling and availability.

The donor undergoes the egg-stimulation and collection procedure; the recipient’s treatment is different. Ask what medicines and visits you personally need, how many eggs or embryos the arrangement includes and what happens if no transferable embryo develops. Donor eggs are an established option after POI, not a guarantee or a compulsory next step.

Donated embryos are a different choice

Embryo donation uses an embryo already created for another person’s or couple’s treatment and donated with the necessary consent. The recipient does not undergo egg collection to create that embryo. Availability, storage history, embryo quality and the information available about the egg and sperm sources can vary; ask exactly what is known.

A donated embryo may have been created with the original patients’ gametes or with previously donated eggs or sperm. Earlier donors’ consent and local rules can therefore matter. Screening records may differ from those available for newly recruited egg donors. A clinic should explain those limits, storage and transfer arrangements, consent requirements and any remaining embryos rather than treating all donations as identical.

Genetic relationship, grief and family conversations

A child’s inherited genetic contribution comes from the egg and sperm used. With an unrelated donor egg and your partner’s sperm, the partner provides a genetic contribution and the person carrying the pregnancy does not provide the egg’s contribution. With an embryo made from two unrelated donors’ gametes, neither intended parent contributes those gametes. A related donor can create a family genetic connection, so broad claims that there is never any relationship are inaccurate.

It is understandable to grieve a hoped-for genetic connection, feel uncertain or decide donation is not right for you. A counsellor experienced in donor conception can help discuss relationships, treatment failure, donor contact and the future child’s interests. Ask about support for early, age-appropriate conversations about origins, without promising how a child will feel. Adoption, other lawful family-building routes or living without children can also be considered without pressure.

Choose a regulated service and understand the donor arrangements

Use a properly regulated clinic and check its credentials before paying or sharing sensitive information. A known friend or relative still needs appropriate assessment. Donor medical and family history, infection tests and genetic screening reduce risk but cannot eliminate it. If a sister is considering egg donation for non-treatment-related POI, ask about shared genetic risk and her own ovarian response.

Do not assume a donor will remain anonymous: laws, access to records and consumer DNA matching can affect future identification. Ask about donor-related siblings, health updates, consent withdrawal and legal parenthood. The rules differ between countries and arrangements; obtain independent advice for your actual situation, especially with known donors or cross-border care. An online matching offer is not evidence of medical screening or legal protection.

Ask for meaningful success estimates

Ask about the chance of live birth with your proposed route, not just fertilisation, a positive test or clinical pregnancy. Clarify whether the figure is per treatment started, egg collection or embryo transfer, and whether several transfers are included. Donor-egg and donated-embryo results should not be treated as one interchangeable statistic.

The age and characteristics of the egg source, embryo development, uterine factors and treatment circumstances matter. Clinic averages reflect the patients selected and may use older data; they are not your personal prognosis. A claim of 90% success after three cycles is not a universal expectation. Ask what happens after a failed cycle and agree when to review the plan rather than assuming further attempts must succeed.

Compare the complete costs

There is no universal rule that donated embryos are cheaper than donor eggs, that frozen donor eggs always save money or that a particular route is affordable. Availability, local funding, medicines, screening and the number of attempts change the total. Ask for a written estimate for your actual plan, including what is refundable if treatment is cancelled.

Check consultation, donor matching, tests, counselling, legal advice where needed, medicines, laboratory work, transfer, storage, transport and later attempts. Compare like with like and allow for travel and time away from work. Expensive add-ons should have a clear explanation of benefit, uncertainty and harm. Intraovarian PRP sold as ovarian rejuvenation has no reliable evidence of benefit and raises safety concerns; paying more does not guarantee a better outcome.

Assess the health of the person carrying the pregnancy

An egg source and the ability to carry a pregnancy are separate questions. Before transfer, review the uterus, medical history, medicines and relevant preconception tests. POI does not automatically mean a gestational carrier is needed. If the uterus is absent or pregnancy would be unsafe, discuss other options and their medical, legal and emotional implications where available.

Pregnancy with donor eggs needs appropriate obstetric care because risks are higher; a younger donor does not remove the recipient’s health risks. Prior uterine radiation or Turner syndrome requires particular assessment. Previous anthracycline treatment or cardiac irradiation can require cardiology input. Tell the maternity team about donor conception and previous treatment so the pregnancy plan reflects the actual history.

Hormone care and contraception remain important

POI care continues whether or not you pursue pregnancy. Hormone replacement often helps replace missing hormones and protect health until the usual menopause age, unless unsuitable for your circumstances. A person with a uterus generally needs appropriate progestogen with systemic estrogen. Cancer history and other risks require an individual plan; do not start, stop or change hormones to try to restore fertility yourself.

HRT is not contraception. If pregnancy is unwanted and ovarian activity is possible, discuss a reliable method. A suitable combined contraceptive pill can prevent pregnancy and may also provide hormone replacement; POI does not make ordinary contraceptive pills inherently ineffective. Suitability, correct use and interactions still matter. Ask how contraception fits with HRT rather than combining regimens yourself.

Make a plan, and know when symptoms need care

Bring previous results, treatment and storage records, medicines and your questions to the appointment. Ask about realistic options, time, costs, support and a second opinion if helpful. During fertility treatment, contact the clinic promptly for abdominal pain or bloating, nausea or vomiting, feeling faint, coughing blood, vaginal bleeding or brown watery discharge, or pain with passing urine or stool. Do not dismiss possible pregnancy because you have POI.

During fertility treatment, get emergency care for breathing difficulty, chest or upper-back pain, marked thirst with reduced urine, swelling anywhere in the body, one-sided lower abdominal pain or shoulder-tip pain. Sudden intense abdominal pain with very severe dizziness, fainting or nausea can indicate a ruptured ectopic pregnancy and also needs emergency help. Do not wait for every sign, a positive pregnancy test or an app entry, and do not drive yourself if seriously unwell. Follow the clinic’s own emergency instructions as well.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask the team to explain the diagnosis and compare own stored material, any remaining ovarian activity and donor options in your circumstances.

Request an individual live-birth estimate, written complete costs and counselling about donors, consent and the child’s future interests.

Agree on ongoing hormone care, contraception or pregnancy planning, and keep the clinic’s urgent contact instructions.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you keep questions, cycle changes and appointment notes together. It cannot diagnose POI, predict ovarian recovery or treatment success, select a donor or hormone regimen, or decide that concerning symptoms can wait.

When to seek help

Do not self-prescribe fertility hormones or ovarian rejuvenation treatments. HRT is not contraception. During fertility treatment, use emergency care for breathing difficulty, chest or upper-back pain, marked thirst with reduced urine, body swelling, one-sided lower abdominal pain or shoulder-tip pain. Sudden intense abdominal pain with severe dizziness, fainting or nausea also needs emergency assessment. Do not wait for all signs or a positive test; contact the clinic promptly for other concerning treatment symptoms.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • POI substantially reduces natural fertility, but non-surgical POI can include intermittent ovarian activity.
  • Stored own eggs or embryos, donor eggs and donated embryos have different requirements and uncertainties.
  • Ask for live-birth estimates and complete written costs; no route guarantees success.
  • Counselling, donor screening, consent and the future child’s interests belong in the decision.
  • HRT is not contraception; agree on a suitable plan whether pregnancy is wanted or not.

Frequently asked questions

Can someone with POI become a parent?

Options can include pregnancy using intermittent own ovarian activity, previously stored eggs or embryos, or donor treatment when suitable. Other family-building choices may also be considered. Diagnosis, health, access and personal wishes determine the discussion; donation is not compulsory.

Are donor eggs always successful?

No. Donor eggs are an established option, but fertilisation, embryo development, implantation and live birth are separate stages. Ask for an individual estimate and the denominator behind any clinic figure, not a universal 90% promise.

Is embryo donation always cheaper?

No. Compare full written costs for the actual arrangements, including tests, medication, counselling, legal advice where needed, transfer, storage and repeat attempts. Funding and availability differ, and a low advertised price may omit important costs.

Will a donor-conceived child be genetically related to us?

It depends on whose egg and sperm created the embryo. A partner whose sperm is used contributes genetically. With two unrelated donors’ gametes, neither intended parent contributes those gametes; a related donor can create an extended-family link. Appearance cannot be guaranteed.

Can I use eggs frozen before cancer treatment?

Possibly, if suitable eggs or embryos remain in storage and the consent and treatment requirements are met. Their prospects depend partly on age at collection and the material stored. Oncology and fertility teams should review timing and pregnancy safety; storage is not a guarantee.

Does a returning period or hormone treatment mean fertility has recovered?

No. Bleeding can occur without reliable ovulation, and HRT replaces hormones rather than proving ovarian recovery. No intervention has reliably restored natural conception rates in POI. Discuss any proposed own-egg attempt and its realistic limits with a specialist.

Do I still need contraception?

If pregnancy is unwanted and ovarian activity is possible, yes. HRT does not prevent pregnancy. A suitable contraceptive pill or another method can be considered according to health, preferences, correct use and interactions; do not select or combine hormone regimens yourself.

Must I decide about donation immediately?

No. Ask what timing matters medically, then take supported time to consider the options. Counselling and a second opinion can help with genetic connection, costs, donor arrangements and possible treatment failure. You may pause or decline a route without having to justify your wishes.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
